1198.title: The storehouse
1198.hook: the storehouse consciousness where the seeds of habit are kept (Lankavatara)
1198.howItsDone: In Yogacara study, and in East Asian and Tibetan schools that inherited it, the storehouse consciousness and its seeds are taught as a way to understand how habits and karma carry forward from moment to moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a finger pointed at the moon, and the trick was to look past it. Your line: not the finger.

Why do the same words come out in the same argument, year after year? Nobody sits down at the kitchen table and decides to say them again. They're just there, ready, before anyone has thought anything at all. The Lankavatara Sutra, and the Yogacara teachers who worked with the same ideas, gave a name to the place where that readiness waits, out of sight. It came up briefly with mind only; today it gets a day of its own.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS, THE SAME FIGHT.` → `READY BEFORE ANY THOUGHT.` → `WHERE DOES IT WAIT?`

segments.voice: The name is alaya-vijnana, usually translated storehouse consciousness. Yogacara teachers described the mind in layers. On top, the ones everyone knows: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the thinking mind that sorts it all out. Under those, a layer that quietly keeps insisting there's a fixed self in charge. And beneath everything, the storehouse. What's kept there? Seeds; that's the word these teachers used. Every action, every word, every thought leaves a seed behind. The seed sits there, unseen. Then one day the conditions are right, a certain tone of voice, a certain tired evening, and the seed ripens. Out comes the reaction, fully formed, as if from nowhere, and that ripening plants new seeds of its own. That's how a habit keeps itself going. The Lankavatara has a picture for this: the storehouse is like the ocean, and the other kinds of consciousness are like waves, stirred up by the wind of what is seen and heard. The waves and the ocean are not two separate things. Buddhist schools have argued about this idea. Some worried that a storehouse sounds too much like a hidden, permanent self. Yogacara teachers answered that it's a stream, never the same from one moment to the next, more like a river than a box. And the teaching runs the other way too. Seeds can be planted on purpose. A kind word leaves a seed. So does a pause, a breath before answering, one honest apology. Those seeds also wait in the dark, and they also ripen, sometimes long after anyone remembers planting them.
screen: `A STOREHOUSE UNDER THE MIND.` · `EVERY ACT LEAVES A SEED.` · `AN OCEAN AND ITS WAVES.` · `SEEDS PLANTED ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `SEEDS IN THE STOREHOUSE.`

segments.voice: Sit for a moment and notice how many reactions come up on their own: an itch, a plan, a little worry. Those are seeds ripening; let them pass. Then picture one small good act, a thank-you or a slower reply, and let the intention sink down like a seed pressed into soil.
The storehouse. Alaya-vijnana, the deep layer of mind where, Yogacara teaches, the seeds of every action wait to ripen. Today's word.
Your line: seeds in the storehouse. Some of them were planted on purpose. That's today, done.

1199.title: The Medicine Buddha
1199.hook: the blue healing Buddha and his twelve vows
1199.howItsDone: In Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese and Tibetan Buddhism, people recite the Medicine Buddha's name, sutra or mantra for those who are ill, and some temples hold Medicine Buddha services for the sick and the dying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the storehouse, where every act leaves a seed that ripens later. Your line: seeds in the storehouse.

Deep blue. That's the first thing about him in paintings and statues: a body the color of lapis lazuli, the stone that looks like a night sky with a little gold in it. Some images show him holding a bowl or a jar of medicine in his lap. Back in year two, the Buddha was a physician who diagnoses first. Here is a whole Buddha of medicine, and the thing his sutra keeps returning to isn't a philosophy. It's sickness, and people with no one to care for them.
screen: `A BODY OF LAPIS BLUE.` → `A BOWL OF MEDICINE.` → `A BUDDHA FOR THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Bhaisajyaguru means medicine master, or medicine teacher. His sutra gives him a longer name too, with the light of lapis lazuli in it, and says he presides over a pure land of his own, far off in the east. Then it tells how he got there. Long ago, while he was still a bodhisattva on the path, he made twelve great vows. That's the heart of it. Here are a few, in plain words. He vowed that his body would shine like lapis, bright inside and out, so people lost in the dark could find their way by it. He vowed that those who are sick, with no doctor, no medicine, no family, no home, would hear his name, and their sickness would ease, and they'd find what they lacked. He vowed that the hungry would be fed, that people without clothes would be clothed, and that people in trouble, bound or afraid, would be set free. And the healing is wide. Some vows are about bodies. Others are about minds: people caught in wrong views, people who've broken their own commitments, people who can't seem to find their way back. The sutra treats all of that as illness too, and all of it as something to be healed. So where the Medicine Buddha is honored, people turn to him when someone is sick: they recite his name or his mantra, or make offerings for a friend in the hospital. A hospital ward is an ordinary place, full of ordinary waiting. His vows are made for exactly that place.
screen: `MEDICINE MASTER, LAPIS LIGHT.` · `TWELVE GREAT VOWS.` · `FOR THE SICK WITH NO DOCTOR.` · `BODIES, AND MINDS TOO.` · then, large: `THE HEALING BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: Find one place in your body that aches or feels tired, and silently wish it ease. Then widen the wish the way the vows widen: someone in a hospital tonight with no visitors, someone hungry, someone caught in thinking that keeps hurting them, each with a breath and the words may it ease. If you practice this path, you can recite the Medicine Buddha's name; if not, the wish is enough.
Bhaisajyaguru. The Medicine Buddha, deep blue as lapis, whose twelve vows are for the sick and the forgotten. Today's word.
Your line: the healing Buddha. Blue as a night sky, with a little gold in it. See you tomorrow.

1200.title: Ksitigarbha's vow
1200.hook: the bodhisattva vows not to rest until the hell realms are empty
1200.howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese Buddhism, Ksitigarbha is honored as the bodhisattva of the lower realms, and his sutra is often recited for parents and loved ones who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Medicine Buddha, deep blue, with vows for the sick who have no one. Your line: the healing Buddha.

Until the hells are empty, I will not become a Buddha. That's the vow, in the short form it's carried in, of a bodhisattva named Ksitigarbha. A promise usually comes with an end in sight: until the project's done, until the kids are grown, until the debt is paid. This one is built so that the end may never come. And the one who made it, in the story his sutra tells, started out as a grieving daughter.
screen: `UNTIL THE HELLS ARE EMPTY.` → `A PROMISE WITH NO END IN SIGHT.` → `IT BEGINS WITH A DAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: The Sutra of Ksitigarbha's Original Vows tells several stories of his past lives. Here's one. Long ago, in the time of an earlier Buddha, there lived a young woman of a brahmin family, devoted and kind. Her mother was not. Her mother mocked the teaching and the Buddha, and then she died. The daughter was afraid of where her mother's actions would carry her. So she sold what she had, made offerings, and gave herself to devotion to the Buddha of that age, calling on him with her whole heart. In the sutra's telling, she was taken to the edge of the hell realms, a sea of suffering, and she saw what was there. A guardian told her that her mother had already been freed, because of the merit of her daughter's devotion. Her mother was safe. Here's the turn. She didn't go home relieved. She had seen everyone else still down there. So she vowed, before that Buddha, to spend lifetimes freeing every being who suffered in those places. That young woman, the sutra says, became Ksitigarbha. A private grief, for one person, opens out into a promise for everyone. He's the bodhisattva who goes down into the lowest places, the ones others would rather not look at. In art he's often a monk with a shaved head, holding a staff with rings and a jewel; some say the staff opens the gates and the jewel lights up the dark. Some read the vow as holding back his own awakening. Others hear that his awakening and everyone else's are tied together, and he won't untie them.
screen: `A DAUGHTER FEARS FOR HER MOTHER.` · `SHE SEES THE LOW PLACES.` · `ONE GRIEF BECOMES A VOW.` · `A STAFF, AND A LIGHT IN THE DARK.` · then, large: `NOT UNTIL ALL ARE FREE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone in a place most people would rather not look at: a person sleeping in a doorway, someone in prison, a relative the family has stopped calling. Notice the pull to look away, and don't fight it; just come back and stay with them for one more breath, then another.
Ksitigarbha's vow. The bodhisattva's promise not to become a Buddha until the hell realms are empty. Today's word.
Your line: not until all are free. If grief is heavy for you today, you don't have to carry it alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help. Twelve hundred days.

1201.title: Jizo by the road
1201.hook: in Japan Ksitigarbha is Jizo, protector of travelers and of children who have died
1201.howItsDone: In Japan, people leave offerings at Jizo figures by roads and in temple grounds, and some temples hold memorial rites in which parents who have lost a child or a pregnancy dress Jizo figures in red bibs and caps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ksitigarbha's vow, born from one daughter's grief: no rest while anyone is left in the low places. Your line: not until all are free.

A small stone figure stands at the edge of a mountain path in Japan. Round, shaved head. Eyes half closed. Someone has tied a red bib around its neck and put a knitted red cap on its head, carefully, the way you'd dress a toddler for cold weather. There's a coin at its feet, an orange, and a plastic pinwheel turning in the wind. Nobody is around. This is yesterday's bodhisattva, under the name Japanese Buddhists know him by.
screen: `A STONE FIGURE BY A PATH.` → `A RED CAP, A RED BIB.` → `A PINWHEEL IN THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Jizo is the Japanese way of reading the name Ksitigarbha, as it was written in Chinese. Same bodhisattva, same vow to go into the low places. But in Japan he has come down to the side of the road: small, close, easy to reach. He's a protector of travelers. Jizo figures stand at crossroads, along paths, at the edges of villages and mountain passes, where people come and go and a journey can turn. A traveler can stop, bow, leave something small, and walk on. And he's a protector of children, especially children who have died. This is where yesterday's vow becomes very tender. There's a story people tell, carried in old Japanese hymns. Children who die young go to a riverbank in the next world, where they pile up little towers of stones as offerings for the parents they left behind. Demons come and knock the towers down. And Jizo comes. He gathers the children up, hides them in the sleeves of his robe, and keeps them safe. So parents who have lost a child, including a pregnancy that ended too soon, sometimes come to a Jizo figure to remember. They tie on the bib, set down a toy, stack a few stones. Some say the red cloth is for protection, others that it simply dresses him like a child; the meanings vary from place to place. Each one is an act of care. A vow from a sutra, about suffering in the lowest places, has become a stone figure you can kneel beside, small enough to dress with your own hands.
screen: `KSITIGARBHA, CALLED JIZO.` · `AT THE CROSSROADS.` · `A RIVERBANK OF SMALL STONES.` · `A BIB TIED ON BY HAND.` · then, large: `THE PROTECTOR OF CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small roadside shrine you know: a memorial by a road, flowers tied to a fence, a plaque on a bench, a statue in a garden. Think of whoever put it there and whoever it's for, without needing to know their names. If you'd like, imagine setting one small stone beside it.
Jizo. Ksitigarbha as Japan knows him: the small figure by the road, guardian of travelers and of children who have died. Today's word.
Your line: the protector of children. If a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Until tomorrow, gently.

1202.title: Hearing inward
1202.hook: Avalokiteshvara's practice of turning hearing back to its source (Surangama)
1202.howItsDone: In Chinese Buddhism and in some Chan and Zen communities, Avalokiteshvara's practice of turning the hearing around is taught as a meditation method, and the passage from the Surangama Sutra is studied and recited.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jizo, the small stone figure by the road in a red bib, guarding travelers and children who have died. Your line: the protector of children.

Somewhere near you, a sound is going on right now. A fan, a car passing, a voice in another room. It arrived without being asked. Ears don't have lids. Now a stranger question: what is it that hears the sound? Not the sound, and not quite the ear. The hearing. In a Mahayana sutra called the Surangama, a bodhisattva says his whole path opened when he turned that question around. He is Avalokiteshvara, the one who hears the cries of the world.
screen: `A SOUND IS GOING ON RIGHT NOW.` → `WHAT HEARS IT?` → `THE ONE WHO HEARS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha puts a plain question to a gathering of awakened beings: how did each of you break through? The answers differ. One woke through sight. One through a fragrance drifting in the air. One through the feel of bath water on the skin. Avalokiteshvara answers: through hearing. He began by listening. Then, instead of following each sound outward, he turned the hearing back toward its source. One English rendering of the sutra's phrase is entering the stream and forgetting the place. Sounds kept coming and going. Then even the coming and going fell quiet, sound and silence both, and still the hearing was there, untouched by either. It fits him. In Chinese he is Guanyin, a name the tradition reads as the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In the sutra, the one who learned to listen to listening is the one who can answer every kind of being who calls. After all the answers, the Buddha asks Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, which gate suits the people of this world. Manjushri chooses the gate of the ear. His reasons, in paraphrase: hearing works in every direction at once, through walls, in the dark, with the eyes shut. It doesn't need anything to face. And when a sound ends, the hearing doesn't end with it. The car passes. The street goes quiet. Whatever was hearing the car is now hearing the quiet.
screen: `HOW DID EACH OF YOU BREAK THROUGH?` · `HE TURNED THE HEARING BACK.` · `GUANYIN: THE ONE WHO HEARS.` · `MANJUSHRI CHOOSES THE EAR.` · then, large: `SOUND GOES. HEARING STAYS.`

segments.voice: Let the eyes close or soften, and for a little while just listen: sounds near and far, loud and faint, without naming them. Then gently turn around, and instead of reaching for the next sound, notice the listening itself, open and already here. When a sound pulls you out, hear it and turn back, and in the gaps between sounds, notice that hearing is still on.
Hearing inward. In the Surangama Sutra, Avalokiteshvara's way: listening, then turning the hearing back toward its source. Today's word.
Your line: turn the hearing around. Any sound, a siren or a ringtone, can work like a bell. See you tomorrow.

1203.title: Gold in rags
1203.hook: Buddha-nature like gold wrapped in dirty rags, or honey guarded by bees (Tathagatagarbha Sutra)
1203.howItsDone: In East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism, the similes of the Tathagatagarbha Sutra are used in teaching about Buddha-nature, and teachers point to them when encouraging respect for every being.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Avalokiteshvara in the Surangama, listening, then listening to listening. Your line: turn the hearing around.

A lump of baked clay sits on a workshop floor, black from the furnace, cracked, the kind of thing you'd sweep out with the ashes. A smith picks it up and taps it with a hammer. The clay falls away in pieces. Inside is a statue of the Buddha, cast in gold. The mold was only what the gold was poured into. That picture sits in a short Mahayana sutra, the Tathagatagarbha, beside another: a golden statue wrapped in filthy rags.
screen: `A BLACKENED LUMP OF CLAY.` → `ONE TAP OF THE HAMMER.` → `GOLD INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Back on day eleven hundred two, this path met the teaching itself: every living being carries Buddha-nature, covered but never lost. Today, how the sutra paints it, and what the pictures ask of the one looking. The rags: a traveler carries a golden statue through rough country and dies on the road. The statue lies in the dirt in rotten cloth. People step over it; nobody passing by sees what it is. Someone with clear eyes has to see it and have it unwrapped. The bees: honey hangs in a tree, guarded by a swarm. Someone who wants it doesn't attack the honey. They find a skillful way past the bees. The house: a poor family lives over buried treasure. The treasure can't speak up and say, I'm here, so they stay poor, standing on gold. The woman: a poor, lonely woman, looked down on by everyone, carries a child who will become a king. She doesn't know it. She thinks of herself the way the street thinks of her. Lay them side by side and a pattern shows. The covering is real: rags rot, bees sting, poverty hurts. And the treasure can't announce itself. Someone has to see past the covering, and the sutra says that's what a Buddha does, looking at beings and seeing what they carry. The rags don't make the statue less gold. They just make it very easy to step over.
screen: `THE STATUE IN THE RAGS.` · `THE HONEY AND THE BEES.` · `TREASURE UNDER A POOR HOUSE.` · `A POOR WOMAN CARRYING A KING.` · then, large: `THE TREASURE CAN'T SPEAK UP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose rags are obvious to you, rude, careless, worn out, hard to like, and notice the rags plainly, without pretending they aren't there. Then gently look past them, the way the smith looks at the clay. You don't need to see the gold clearly; only allow that it might be there.
Gold in rags. In the Tathagatagarbha Sutra, a golden Buddha statue wrapped in filthy cloth: a picture of Buddha-nature, covered but never lost. Today's word.
Your line: gold in the rags. Covered is not the same as lost. Until tomorrow.

1204.title: Queen Srimala
1204.hook: a queen teaches before the Buddha, and he approves (Srimaladevi Sutra)
1204.howItsDone: The Srimaladevi Sutra is studied in East Asian Buddhism, especially in teaching on Buddha-nature, and Srimala is remembered as a lay teacher who preached in the Buddha's presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the clay mold that broke open on gold, and the statue nobody saw under its rags. Your line: gold in the rags.

A letter arrives at a palace in Ayodhya. It's from the queen's parents, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallika. They have met the Buddha, they write, and they want their daughter to know about him too. Queen Srimala reads it, and something in her opens. She answers not with a letter but with verses of praise, spoken aloud, and in the sutra the Buddha appears in the sky over the palace to hear her. Then the surprise. She doesn't just listen. She teaches, and he says, go on.
screen: `A LETTER FROM HER PARENTS.` → `SHE ANSWERS WITH PRAISE.` → `THE BUDDHA APPEARS.`

segments.voice: Before she teaches anything, Srimala makes vows in front of the Buddha, and they are strikingly practical. Not to give way to anger toward any being. Not to envy what others have. Not to hoard for herself. And when she meets the lonely, the imprisoned, the sick and the poor, not to walk away until she has helped. Then she asks permission to speak, and he gives it. In the sutra the queen does most of the talking. The Buddha's part is often to listen and approve, saying, in substance, excellent, excellent, just so. Her subject is large: holding fast to the true teaching, that the many vehicles of the path are finally one, and the Buddha-nature hidden in beings, the same gold from yesterday's rags. A laywoman, a married queen, sets out weighty Mahayana teaching, and the sutra shows the Buddha confirming it point by point. Then the title: the Lion's Roar of Queen Srimala. The lion's roar is a phrase Buddhist texts use for the Buddha's own fearless teaching. Here it is given to her. She closes a week that ran from the storehouse of seeds through the healing Buddha, Ksitigarbha's vow, Jizo by the road, Avalokiteshvara listening and the gold in rags. Srimala ends it with a voice: she speaks, and the Buddha lets her.
screen: `HER VOWS: NO ANGER, NO HOARDING.` · `SHE ASKS TO SPEAK.` · `ONE VEHICLE, HIDDEN GOLD.` · `THE LION'S ROAR IS HERS.` · then, large: `EXCELLENT, EXCELLENT. JUST SO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman who taught you something that stayed, a grandmother, a teacher, a nurse, a boss, a friend, whether a skill, a way of speaking or a way of carrying trouble. Let her face come clearly, and notice what she gave. If you pray, hold her in that prayer; if you don't, simply hold her in mind with thanks for a while.
Queen Srimala. In the Srimaladevi Sutra, the laywoman and queen who teaches before the Buddha, and whose teaching he approves. Today's word.
Your line: the queen teaches. In this sutra, the lion's roar is hers. That's the week, complete.
